blocks.text: The defeat of Sennacherib, which the sacred writers ascribe to an angel ^{b)}, and Josephus ^{c)}, following Berosus, to a plague sent by God, the Egyptians in Herodotus ^{d)} strangely refer to field mice. They relate that these, τοῖσι ἐναντίοισι αὐτοῖσι ἐπιχυθέντας νυκτὸς, κατὰ μὲν φαγέειν τοὺς φαρετρεῶνας αὐτέων, κατὰ δὲ τὰ τόξα, πρὸς δὲ τῶν ἀσπίδων τὰ ὄχανα· ὥς τε τῇ ὑστεραίῃ φευγόντων σφέων, γυμνῶν ὅπλων, πεσέειν πολλούς· [toisi enantioisi autoisi epichythentas nyktos, kata men phagein tous pharetreōnas autеōn, kata de ta toxa, pros de tōn aspidōn ta ochana; hōs te tē hysteraiē pheugontōn sphеōn, gymnōn hoplōn, pesеein pollous] poured over the enemy themselves by night, gnawed through their quivers, their bows, and the handles of their shields, so that the next day, stripped of their arms and with many lost, they took to flight. Is it relevant here that λοιμὸς [loimos] plague and λαμὰς [lamas] mouse in Hesychius are words so close that one could have been used for the other, and thus a defeat brought about by plague was ascribed to mice? However that may be, something of the kind is recorded to have happened to those Cretans who founded Hamaxitus, a city of the Troad. For when Apollo [II, 435], consulted about where to found their city, had answered that it must be founded ἔνθα ἂν αὐτοῖς οἱ γηγενεῖς πολεμήσωσι [entha an autois hoi gēgeneis polemēsōsi], where the earth-born should make war on them, they understood that Hamaxitus was meant; because, when they had pitched camp there, μυῶν ἄφατόν τι πλῆθος ἐφερπύσαν τά τε ὄχανα αὐτοῖς τῶν ἀσπίδων διέτραγε, καὶ τὰς τῶν τόξων νευρὰς διέφαγεν [myōn aphaton ti plēthos epherpysan ta te ochana autois tōn aspidōn dietrage, kai tas tōn toxōn neuras diephagen], an immense host of mice, bursting forth, gnawed the handles of their shields and ate through the strings of their bows. So Aelian, History, book 12, chapter 5. Not very differently the old Scholiast of Homer on book 1 of the Iliad: Νυκτὸς ἐπιγενομένης, μῦες ἔκοψαν αὐτῶν τοὺς τελαμῶνας τῶν ὅπλων [Nyktos epigenomenēs, myes ekopsan autōn tous telamōnas tōn hoplōn], When night had come, mice cut through the straps of their arms. Accordingly, in Aristotle, Rhetoric, book 2, chapter 24, Polycrates praises mice ὅτι ἐβοήθησαν διατραγόντες τὰς νευρὰς [hoti eboēthēsan diatragontes tas neuras], because they brought help (to his countrymen) when they gnawed through the strings of the enemy's bows. And in Clement's Protrepticus, Polemo reports that the peoples neighbouring the Troad τοὺς ἐπιχωρίους μῦς, οὓς σμίνθους καλοῦσι θρησβεύειν, ὅτι τὰς νευρὰς τῶν πολεμίων διέτρωγον τῶν τόξων· [tous epichōrious mys, hous sminthous kalousi thrēsbeuein, hoti tas neuras tōn polemiōn dietrōgon tōn toxōn] worship the mice of that place, which they call sminthoi, because they had gnawed the strings of the enemy's bows. Since these accounts are very similar to what the Egyptians relate of the Assyrians, I would think that they worked this Cretan, or if you prefer Trojan, story into their own.
